To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

colorectal carcinoma in patients ≤40 year of age is a rare but not infrequent diagnosis and is not frequently associated with underlying Lynch syndrome, chronic inflammatory bowel disease, or other cancer-predisposition genetic disorders.

colorectal carcinoma in patients ≤40 years of age is a distinct clinical and pathological entity with an increased incidence in the sigmoid colon and the rectum, and is associated with an increased incidence of adverse histologic factors and a higher rate of metastatic disease.

early onset colorectal carcinoma (≤40 years) is a distinct clinicopathologic entity characterized by rectal and sigmoid location, adverse morphologic features (signet ring cell differentiation), and frequent metastatic disease.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
colorectal carcinoma in the young is not uncommon, but is not frequently the manifestation of a known genetic syndrome.
colorectal carcinoma diagnosed in patients ≤ 40 years of ages is associated with a higher incidence of adverse histologic factors compared with colorectal carcinoma diagnosed at older ages.
colorectal carcinoma diagnosed in young patients is not a distinct entity, but rather a group of tumors with distinct clinicopathologic and molecular characteristics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
early-onset colorectals should be considered in the differential diagnosis of colorectal carcinoma and that the tumors may be more aggressive than the typical older adult colorectal carcinoma.
